answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — actually Dale Carnegie
answer.sourceLine: The line is Dale Carnegie’s own, from How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936), Part One, Chapter 1. Because Carnegie is discussing Benjamin Franklin’s tact on the surrounding pages, the aphorism drifted onto Franklin’s name—but Franklin never wrote it (CheckYourFact ↗).

source.excerpt: Any fool can criticize, condemn and complain — and most fools do. But it takes character and self-control to be understanding and forgiving.
trail: CheckYourFact ↗ rates the Franklin attribution false and names Carnegie’s 1936 book as the source.

source.excerptNote: Carnegie’s own words, immediately after his discussion of Benjamin Franklin’s diplomacy—the proximity is what spawned the false Franklin credit. Some reprints reorder it as “criticize, complain, and condemn.”
source.rightsNote: How to Win Friends and Influence People was first published in 1936 by Simon & Schuster, so in the United States the text remains under copyright (works published 1931–1977 run 95 years from publication). The wording is Carnegie’s, not a public-domain Franklin line.

author.name: Dale Carnegie
author.heading: About Dale Carnegie
author.metaLine: 1888–1955 · American writer & lecturer, author of How to Win Friends and Influence People
author.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and public-speaking teacher whose 1936 bestseller How to Win Friends and Influence People became one of the most influential self-improvement books ever written. His first principle—“Don’t criticize, condemn, or complain”—is the setting for this aphorism, which is his own gloss on the idea. He often illustrated his points with historical figures like Benjamin Franklin, which is precisely how his lines came to be mistaken for theirs.

misattribution.heading: Why Franklin gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is routinely pinned on Benjamin Franklin across social media, quote sites, and posters—but the attribution is a documented error.

items.why: Franklin never wrote or said this. Carnegie discusses Franklin’s diplomatic manner on the very pages where the line appears, and readers collapsed the two—crediting Franklin with Carnegie’s own commentary (CheckYourFact ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Dale Carnegie’s, from How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936), and are listed in the sourced section of his Wikiquote page ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Carnegie built his book’s opening principle—“Don’t criticize, condemn, or complain”—around the idea that criticism is easy and useless. This one-liner is his sharpest compression of that lesson: the “fool” framing turns a self-help maxim into a memorable jab.

Its migration to Benjamin Franklin is a textbook case of how proximity breeds misattribution: a modern author quotes an admired historical figure, and over time the famous name absorbs the modern line.
